1002.title: Take off your shoes
1002.hook: at the burning bush, Moses is told the ground is holy (Exodus 3:1–5)
1002.howItsDone: Muslims remove their shoes before praying in a mosque, and shoes come off in Hindu and Sikh temples too; Jews and Christians read the burning bush in Exodus 3 as the moment Moses is called.

segments.voice: Yesterday, consider the lilies, and a wildflower dressed better than a king. Your line was consider the lilies. Which small living thing did you look at? Today, awe arrives on an ordinary workday. Day one thousand two.

Moses isn't looking for anything. Exodus sets the scene plainly, in the King James words: "Now Moses kept the flock of Jethro his father in law, the priest of Midian: and he led the flock to the backside of the desert". A shepherd, at work, far from anywhere, with someone else's sheep. Then, at the edge of his vision, a bush on fire. The fire itself isn't the strange part. The strange part is what it isn't doing. Today, a story about the moment someone stops walking, and about what he's told to do with his feet.
screen: `A SHEPHERD AT WORK.` → `A BUSH ON FIRE.` → `WHAT IT ISN'T DOING.`

segments.voice: First, the sight. Exodus says "the bush burned with fire, and the bush was not consumed." Fire that doesn't use anything up. A plain thing doing something it shouldn't. Second, the turn. Moses says: "I will now turn aside, and see this great sight, why the bush is not burnt." He leaves the path. He stops herding long enough to look. And the next line is the hinge of the story: "And when the LORD saw that he turned aside to see, God called unto him out of the midst of the bush". In the text, the call comes after the turning aside. Third, the instruction: "Draw not nigh hither: put off thy shoes from off thy feet, for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground." Notice where the holiness is. Not in a temple. Exodus calls this Horeb, the mountain of God, but Moses came there with sheep, not to worship. In the dirt under his own feet, at his ordinary work. Fourth, the gesture. Taking off shoes is a way the body says: this place is different, and I'm not in charge here. In mosques, shoes come off before prayer, and the Qur'an tells the same story, with Moses told to take off his shoes in the holy valley. Some homes ask guests to leave their shoes at the door. The feet go bare, and the ground can be felt.
screen: `A FIRE THAT DOESN'T CONSUME.` · `HE TURNED ASIDE TO SEE.` · `UNDER HIS OWN FEET.` · `SHOES OFF, GROUND FELT.` · then, large: `HOLY GROUND.`

segments.voice: If you can, take off your shoes, and socks too if that's comfortable, and stand. If standing isn't possible, sit and rest your bare feet on the floor. Let the breath settle. Feel what's under you: cool tile, rough carpet, wood, grass, warm concrete. Feel the weight move through the heels and the balls of the feet. This is the ground you were already standing on before the lesson began. Let it be, for two minutes, a place that matters. If you pray, you can let the standing be your prayer. If not, let it be your attention. The bell holds the time.
Take off your shoes. What Moses is told at the burning bush, because the ordinary ground under his feet is holy. Today's word.
Your line: holy ground. When you take off your shoes tonight, pause one breath on the bare floor and say the line to yourself. Day one thousand two.

fork.reveal: he turns aside to see, and only then does God call to him from the bush.

1003.title: The still small voice
1003.hook: not in the wind, earthquake or fire, but a still small voice (1 Kings 19:11–12)
1003.howItsDone: Jews and Christians read Elijah's story in 1 Kings 19 as a teaching about how God speaks; some people take it as a reason to sit in silence and listen.

segments.voice: Yesterday, take off your shoes, and Moses at the bush that wasn't consumed. Your line was holy ground. Did you stand barefoot for a breath last night? Today, a prophet who expected fire and got something else. Day one thousand three.

Elijah is done. In the book of Kings, Queen Jezebel has sworn to kill the prophet. He runs into the wilderness, sits under a juniper tree, and asks to die. An angel wakes him, feeds him, and he walks on until he reaches a mountain and goes into a cave. And there a voice asks him a strange question: "What doest thou here, Elijah?" Then he's told to go out and stand on the mountain, because the LORD is about to pass by. What comes next is a scene of startling quiet.
screen: `ELIJAH IS DONE.` → `A CAVE ON THE MOUNTAIN.` → `WHAT DOEST THOU HERE?`

segments.voice: First, the noise. In the King James words: "and, behold, the LORD passed by, and a great and strong wind rent the mountains, and brake in pieces the rocks before the LORD; but the LORD was not in the wind: and after the wind an earthquake; but the LORD was not in the earthquake". Then a fire, and again: not in the fire. Wind, earthquake, fire: the things that usually announce power. Each one arrives, and each one is empty. Second, the quiet: "and after the fire a still small voice." That's it. No thunder, no blaze. Some readers hear the Hebrew as something even quieter than a voice: a thin silence. Whatever it was, it was small. Third, Elijah's response. He's been through the wind and the earthquake, but it's the quiet that moves him. The text says that when Elijah heard it, he wrapped his face in his mantle and went out and stood at the mouth of the cave. Awe, here, comes in at a whisper. Fourth, why it matters on an ordinary day. A lot of life is wind and earthquake and fire: notifications, headlines, arguments, alarms. The story suggests that what matters most may not be the loudest thing in the room. For Jews and Christians, this is about how God speaks. For anyone, it's an invitation to make enough quiet to hear something small.
screen: `NOT IN THE WIND, QUAKE OR FIRE.` · `A STILL SMALL VOICE.` · `HE WRAPPED HIS FACE.` · `NOT THE LOUDEST THING.` · then, large: `STILL SMALL VOICE.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and let the noise of the day go by like Elijah's wind. Close your eyes if you like. First, notice the loud things: traffic, a fridge, voices in another room, your own busy thoughts. Don't push them away. Let each one pass by, and let it be not the thing you're listening for. Then listen underneath. The quietest sound you can find. Your breath. The hum of the room. The small silence between two sounds. Stay there. If you pray, you can listen in the way Elijah did, with nothing to say. If you'd like, stay one more minute after the bell. The bell holds the time.
The still small voice. What Elijah heard after the wind, the earthquake and the fire: a quiet so small it moved him more than all the noise. Today's word.
Your line: still small voice. Once today, turn off one noise you could leave on, a radio, a feed, a podcast, and listen to what's left for a minute. Day one thousand three.

what it means: what Elijah heard after wind, earthquake and fire: a quiet that moved him.
what a scholar hears: some readers hear the Hebrew as a thin silence.

1004.title: Holy, holy, holy
1004.hook: Isaiah sees the seraphim calling: holy, holy, holy (Isaiah 6:1–3)
1004.howItsDone: Jews say the seraphim's words in the Kedushah, part of the repeated Amidah prayer, and Christians sing them in the Sanctus at the Eucharist; both come from Isaiah 6:3.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the still small voice, and Elijah hearing the quiet after the fire. Your line was still small voice. What did you hear when one noise went off? Today, the opposite: a vision full of sound. Day one thousand four.

Isaiah dates his vision by a king's death. In the King James words: "In the year that king Uzziah died I saw also the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up, and his train filled the temple." A king has died. And in the temple, Isaiah sees something that fills the room past its edges: the hem of a robe so vast it pours through the whole building. Above the throne stand the seraphim. Today, the word they keep calling to each other, three times over.
screen: `THE YEAR THE KING DIED.` → `HIS TRAIN FILLED THE TEMPLE.` → `THE SERAPHIM.`

segments.voice: First, the seraphim. The text describes them carefully: "each one had six wings; with twain he covered his face, and with twain he covered his feet, and with twain he did fly." Even these beings cover their faces. Awe, in Isaiah, isn't staring. It's knowing you can't quite look. Second, the call: "And one cried unto another, and said, Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts". Not once. Three times, back and forth, as if once couldn't hold it. In Hebrew the word is qadosh. Jewish prayer takes up these words in the Kedushah, and Christian worship sings them in the Sanctus. Third, the second half of the line, the one that's easy to miss: "the whole earth is full of his glory." The holiness isn't kept inside the temple. It spills out, all the way to the edges of the world. Which means the street outside the temple, the market, the field, a kitchen, could all be places where that glory sits. Fourth, the human answer. Isaiah doesn't say how wonderful. He says: "Woe is me! for I am undone". Undone: in the old English sense, ruined, come apart. In the story, one of the seraphim flies to him with a live coal from the altar, touches his lips, and his sin is purged. Awe here takes him apart before it puts him back together. For anyone on this path, the seraphim's line leaves a question: what would it be like to call one ordinary thing holy, and mean it?
screen: `EVEN THE SERAPHIM COVER THEIR FACES.` · `HOLY, HOLY, HOLY.` · `THE WHOLE EARTH IS FULL.` · `WOE IS ME: UNDONE.` · then, large: `HOLY.`

segments.voice: Sit and let the breath settle. Look around and choose one ordinary thing in reach: a cup, a key, your own hand, a window, a chair. Rest your eyes on it. Notice where it came from, who made it, what it has carried or held. Then, quietly or just inside, say one word over it: holy. Not because it's special. Because the seraphim said the whole earth is full, and this is a piece of the earth. Say it once, and let it sit. If you pray, you can say the seraphim's words themselves. If the word feels too big, just look at the thing a little longer. The bell holds the time.
Holy. In Hebrew, qadosh: the word the seraphim call to each other three times in Isaiah's vision, with the whole earth full of glory. Today's word.
Your line: holy, holy, holy. Pick three ordinary things today, one in the morning, one at noon, one at night, and say the word once over each. Day one thousand four.

"with twain he covered his face."

trapdoor: what you thought: holy means very good, or very religious.
what it means: so far beyond us the seraphim cover their faces, and its glory fills the earth.
what a scholar hears: Isaiah dates the vision to a king's death year, and answers it with: I am undone.

1005.title: I knew it not
1005.hook: Jacob wakes: surely the Lord is in this place, and I knew it not (Genesis 28:16)
1005.howItsDone: Jews and Christians read Jacob's dream at Bethel in Genesis 28 as a story of God meeting a person in an unexpected place; some people repeat Jacob's words when they notice an ordinary place anew.

segments.voice: Yesterday, holy, and the seraphim calling it three times. Your line was holy, holy, holy. Which three ordinary things got the word? Today, a man who slept in a holy place without knowing it. Day one thousand five.

A man on the run, alone, with the brother he cheated behind him. That's Jacob in Genesis, long before the day Esau runs to meet him. The sun goes down on him in the middle of nowhere. The King James text is almost offhand: "he lighted upon a certain place, and tarried there all night, because the sun was set". No shrine, nothing to mark it. He takes a stone for a pillow and lies down on the ground. A certain place. Any place. Today, what happens there in the night, and what he says in the morning.
screen: `JACOB ON THE RUN.` → `A CERTAIN PLACE.` → `A STONE FOR A PILLOW.`

segments.voice: First, the dream: "and behold a ladder set up on the earth, and the top of it reached to heaven: and behold the angels of God ascending and descending on it." Notice where the ladder stands. On the earth, right where a tired man is sleeping on a rock. In the dream, heaven isn't somewhere else; it touches down here. Second, the waking. Genesis says: "And Jacob awaked out of his sleep, and he said, Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not." The place didn't change overnight. Jacob did. In his own words, the LORD was in this place when he arrived, when he chose the stone, while he slept. He just didn't know. Third, the fear. The next line: "And he was afraid, and said, How dreadful is this place! this is none other but the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven." Dreadful sounds strange to a modern ear. Here it sits close to awe, the trembling side we met at the start of this block. Fourth, the new name. Jacob sets up his stone as a pillar and calls the place Bethel. Genesis adds that the city had been called Luz before. The same ground, two names: one from before he knew, and one from after. For Jews and Christians, Bethel is a place where God met Jacob. For anyone, it raises a quiet question: how many certain places, ordinary as a roadside, are we passing through without knowing?
screen: `A LADDER SET UP ON THE EARTH.` · `THE PLACE DIDN'T CHANGE. JACOB DID.` · `HOW DREADFUL IS THIS PLACE.` · `LUZ BECOMES BETHEL.` · then, large: `AND I KNEW IT NOT.`

segments.voice: Stay exactly where you are. A room, a car, a bench, a bed. Let the breath settle. Now look at this place as if you'd just woken up in it after a long journey, not knowing where you were. The corners. The light. The sounds. What's worn, what's new, what you've stopped seeing because it's always here. Let the place be a certain place, one you've never quite met. Then, if it feels right, say Jacob's words quietly: and I knew it not. If you pray, you can say the whole line. If not, let the looking be enough. The bell holds the time.
I knew it not. Jacob's words on waking at Bethel: in his telling, the LORD had been there all along, and he was the one who changed. Today's word.
Your line: and I knew it not. Choose one place you pass through every day, a hallway, a bus stop, a doorway, and stop there once today to see it as if for the first time. Day one thousand five.

screen: `DAY 1005 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: SIGNS FOR THOSE WHO THINK.`

1006.title: Signs for those who think
1006.hook: in the heavens and earth and the turning of night and day are signs (Quran 3:190)
1006.howItsDone: Muslims recite the closing verses of Surah Al Imran, and some recite them on waking in the night, following the report that the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ did; reflection on creation is called tafakkur.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jacob waking at Bethel. Your line was and I knew it not. Which everyday place did you see as if for the first time? Today, the Qur'an asks people to look, and to think. Day one thousand six.

Late at night, a man gets up from his bed and looks at the sky. A report in the hadith collection of al-Bukhari tells it this way: Ibn Abbas was staying in the house, and saw the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, wake in the night, look up at the heavens, and recite the closing verses of the Qur'an's third chapter. Those verses begin with the sky, and with the plain fact that night turns into day. Today, a scripture where awe and thinking go together.
screen: `AWAKE IN THE NIGHT.` → `LOOKING AT THE HEAVENS.` → `A SCRIPTURE THAT SAYS: THINK.`

segments.voice: First, the verse. In paraphrase, Surah Al Imran says: in the creation of the heavens and the earth, and in the alternation of night and day, there are signs for people of understanding. Nothing exotic. Sky, ground, and the fact that it gets dark and then light again. Things in plain view, every day. Second, the word signs. In Arabic it's ayat. A sign points past itself, the way a road sign isn't the city but tells you the city is there. In Islamic teaching, the world is full of these pointers, and Muslims use the same word, ayat, for the Qur'an's own verses. The book has signs, and so does the sky. Third, who sees them. The verse doesn't say signs for everyone. It says signs for people of understanding, those who think. The next verse describes them: people who remember God standing, sitting and lying down, and who reflect on the creation of the heavens and the earth, and say: our Lord, you did not create this in vain. Remembering and thinking, together. Awe, here, isn't the end of thought. It's where thought goes when it follows something all the way. Fourth, what it asks of an ordinary day. The turning of night and day happens whether anyone notices or not. The verse asks for noticing, and then for a question: what is this pointing to? For Muslims, the answer is God. For anyone, the turning of the day is still there to watch, and to think about.
screen: `HEAVENS, EARTH, NIGHT AND DAY.` · `AYAT: SIGNS THAT POINT PAST.` · `FOR PEOPLE WHO THINK.` · `NOTICE, THEN ASK.` · then, large: `SIGNS.`

segments.voice: Find the light. A window, a doorway, or simply the way light falls in the room where you are. Let the breath settle. Notice what time of day it is by the light alone, without checking a clock. Is it high and white, low and gold, gray, or electric? Where are the shadows, and which way do they lean? Then ask one quiet question, and don't rush to answer it: what is this pointing to? If you pray, you can remember God as you sit, as the verse describes. If not, let the question stay open. Later today, try to catch the moment the light changes. The bell holds the time.
Signs for those who think. The Qur'an's teaching that the sky, the earth and the turning of night and day are ayat, signs pointing past themselves, for people who reflect. Today's word.
screen: `SIGNS FOR THOSE WHO THINK — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: signs. Watch one turn of the day today, dawn or dusk, from start to finish if you can, and ask what it points to. Day one thousand six.

1007.title: Light upon light
1007.hook: the Verse of Light: God is the light of the heavens and earth, a lamp in a niche
1007.howItsDone: Muslims recite the Verse of Light (Quran 24:35) in prayer and study, and commentators and Sufi writers have reflected on what the niche, the glass, the lamp and the oil might stand for.

segments.voice: Yesterday, signs for those who think: the Quran pointing at the turning of night and day. Your line was signs. Did you catch the light change at the edge of the day? Today we stay with the same book, and with light itself. Day one thousand seven.

A small hollow set into a wall. Inside it, a lamp. Around the flame, a glass so clear it shines like a star. The oil in the lamp comes from an olive tree, and the oil would almost glow on its own, even if no fire touched it. That's the whole scene. A lamp in a niche. It sounds like a room in an old house at night. But it's in the Quran, and it's the likeness the Quran gives for God's light. It's known as the Verse of Light.
screen: `A LAMP IN A NICHE.` → `A GLASS LIKE A STAR.` → `THE VERSE OF LIGHT.`

segments.voice: First, the size of it. The verse opens as big as a sentence can get. In Pickthall's translation: "Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth." Not a light in the sky. The light of all of it. Second, the shrinking. Right after that huge opening, the verse does something surprising. It says it's giving a likeness, a picture, and the picture is tiny: a niche, a lamp, a glass, an olive tree. The verse adds that the tree is neither of the east nor of the west. It belongs to no one direction. So the light that fills everything is shown to us at the size of something you could hold in your two hands. Third, the layers. Look at how the picture is built. The niche holds the lamp. The glass makes the flame shine like a star. The oil is already almost glowing before the fire arrives. Each piece adds to the brightness. And then the verse sums it up in three words: "Light upon light." Fourth, who sees it. The verse goes on to say that God guides to His light whom He will, and that God speaks to people in likenesses. Readers have heard the layers in different ways. Some readers see the niche as the human heart, and the lamp as what shines inside it. Others keep it as a picture of God that no explanation fully opens. The verse itself doesn't decode the picture. It hands you the lamp and lets you look.
screen: `THE LIGHT OF THE HEAVENS AND THE EARTH.` · `SHOWN AT THE SIZE OF A LAMP.` · `NICHE, GLASS, FLAME, OIL.` · `A LIKENESS, NOT A MAP.` · then, large: `LIGHT UPON LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to sit with one lamp. If there's a candle, light it. If there's a lamp, switch it on and turn the others off. If neither, find the brightest small thing in the room, even a patch of daylight on the wall. Let your eyes rest there. Notice the layers: the flame or the bulb, then the glow around it, then the light it throws on the things nearby. Light on light. If you pray, you can hold the verse's opening words. If you don't, simply watch the light do what it does. The bell holds the time.
Light upon light. Three words from the Verse of Light in the Quran, where a lamp in a niche becomes a picture of the light of the heavens and the earth. Today's word.
Your line: light upon light. Tonight, when the lamps come on, notice one light lying on top of another: a lamp on a window, a screen on a face. Day one thousand seven.

1008.title: Wherever you turn
1008.hook: to God belong east and west; wherever you turn, there is God's face
1008.howItsDone: Muslims pray facing the Kaaba in Mecca, and recite verses such as Quran 2:115 to remember that God is not confined to any one direction or place.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the lamp in the niche, and your line was light upon light. This week we've stood on holy ground, listened for a still small voice, heard holy, holy, holy, woken with Jacob, and looked for signs in the turning of the day. Today the week ends with one verse about direction. Day one thousand eight.

Which way does a room face? Most rooms have an answer. A classroom faces the board. A theater faces the stage. A couch, somehow, faces the TV. We arrange ourselves around a front without thinking about it, and when we want to show that something matters, we turn toward it. Now take that habit to the biggest scale there is. If you wanted to face God, which way would you turn? One short verse in the Quran answers that question, and its answer is not a direction on a compass.
screen: `WHICH WAY DOES A ROOM FACE?` → `WE TURN TOWARD WHAT MATTERS.` → `WHICH WAY IS GOD?`

segments.voice: First, the directions themselves. The verse, in Pickthall's translation, begins: "Unto Allah belong the East and the West". East is where the day starts. West is where it ends. Both belong to God. No side of the map is left out. Second, the turn. The verse goes on: "and whithersoever ye turn, there is Allah's Countenance." Whithersoever is an old word for wherever. Turn left, turn right, turn all the way around. The verse doesn't name a place where the turning works and a place where it doesn't. Third, the face. Countenance is Pickthall's word for the Arabic wajh, which means face. A face is not just a surface. It's where someone is present to you, where they're looking back. So some readers hear more here than God being everywhere, like air. They hear a face in every direction, a presence turned toward them. Fourth, how this sits with prayer. Muslims pray facing the Kaaba in Mecca, and a little later in the same chapter the Quran speaks of that direction for prayer. The two sit side by side in one chapter. Prayer has a direction, and the community faces it together. And this verse sets no limit on where God's face is. Some readers put it this way: one is about how people gather, the other about where God can be found. The verse ends by calling God All-Embracing. In the verse's picture, no turn steps outside it.

segments.voice: Today's practice is to turn slowly in a circle. Stand up, if you can, or turn your head and shoulders if you're sitting. Face one way and take a breath. Notice what's there: a wall, a window, a door. Then turn a little, and take another breath. Keep going, slowly, until you've come all the way around. At each stop, hold the verse lightly: wherever you turn. If you pray, you can let each turn be a small greeting. If you don't, just let each direction count as much as the last. The bell holds the time.
Wherever you turn. From the Quran: east and west belong to God, and wherever you turn, there is God's face. Today's word.
